sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
We have only recent data for Zürich's garages, so there is no city trend yet; the figures below are for weekdays in August and September 2026, during the university's summer break.

Zürich's voters have repeatedly backed a gradual squeeze on street parking. The historic parking compromise from the 1990s ended in 2021 [5]. In the same year voters approved a transport master plan that calls for fewer blue-zone spaces [2]. In 2025 they approved new residents' cards priced by vehicle weight, cheaper for electric cars and costing about two to three times the old CHF 300 a year [3][4]. In June 2026 about 59% rejected an initiative that would have allowed street spaces to be removed only if as many stayed available in the district. The city plans to repurpose 9,000–11,000 surface spaces over 10–15 years [5].

Traffic fell sharply in 2020 and 2021. By the end of 2022 public transport was almost back to its 2019 level and cycling was at record highs [12].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
The city has taken its own garages back in-house. Since early 2026 its property department has run the ten municipal garages, ending 17 years of outsourcing to Parking Zürich AG, which the city said could now be formally dissolved; nothing changed for customers [6]. It closed its smallest garage, Central, in 2021 and moved the spaces to the nearby Urania garage [1]. The city parliament has asked the government to look at turning municipal garages into housing [7].

Retail at the top end has changed too: the Jelmoli department store on Bahnhofstrasse closed in February 2025, with Manor due to take three floors from 2027 [13]. Its garage is still well used in our data (49%). Payment and charging have moved on: by 2019 a tenth of on-street parking revenue came through apps [9], and a 2025 test of charging in garages rated Zürich best among the cities tested [11]. The University of Zurich raised its parking fees by 70–150% in 2023, and 220 of 994 long-term contracts at the Irchel garage were cancelled, not all because of the increase [8].

sections.title: Operators, location, price and use
sections.text:
Zürich's garage market is fragmented. The city's garages (still labelled Parking Zürich in our data) are the largest group, at about CHF 3.50 an hour, roughly 10% below their neighbours, and average 40% on weekdays. AMAG Parking runs four central garages at about CHF 5 an hour, above their neighbours, and they are among the fullest (59%). Hotels, department stores and the university run the rest, up to CHF 6 an hour at the Park Hyatt.

Prices step down from about CHF 5 an hour and CHF 45 a day near Paradeplatz to CHF 3 and CHF 28 more than two kilometres out, and occupancy does not follow the centre. The busiest garages are by the lake and at the edge of the old town: Zürichhorn (84%, just as full at weekends), Utoquai (77%), Stampfenbach (76%) and Talgarten (71%). The office districts in the north are the emptiest: the Apleona-run garages in Oerlikon and Leutschenbach stand at 7–20%. The week splits by district. Office garages such as Parkside empty at weekends, while Helvetiaplatz and the Hauptbahnhof garage fill up more on Saturdays and Sundays than on weekdays.
